messages.content: Contemplate on few lines of “Part four” (page 153) of this novel, “Majid: Wake up, Bibi. I am going to take both of you to the village. When Majeed came out of the house carrying Jamila, wrapped in a thin... quilt, a bewilderedRahima at his heels, the brilliant moonlight at first blinded him.” Even if Majeed was mostly depicted as a cunning and apathetic person throughout the narrative, do you find the same character traits in the mentioned lines? Was he trying to save Rahima and Jamila out of good-will (deontology) or his action was well-calculated (teleology)?Explain it. Include at least 10 single-word palindromes, each at least 5 characters long.

message.content:
The scene on page 153 of *Shantay* (often referred to by its protagonist, Majid) presents a stark contrast to the cold pragmatism that usually defines Majid’s character. While he is frequently portrayed as cunning and apathetic, this specific moment reveals a complex layer of his psyche that challenges a purely negative interpretation.

When Majid says, "Wake up, Bibi," and proceeds to take both Rahima and Jamila to the village, his actions are driven by immediate necessity rather than calculated long-term gain. The description of him being blinded by the "brilliant moonlight" suggests a moment of vulnerability and disorientation, stripping away his usual composure. This physical reaction underscores that he is not operating from a place of detached calculation but rather from a raw, urgent instinct to preserve life in a crisis.

Regarding the ethical framework, Majid’s action leans heavily toward **teleology** (consequentialism) rather than deontology (duty-based ethics). Deontology would imply he is saving them because it is his moral duty or right as a husband/father figure, regardless of the outcome. However, Majid has consistently shown a lack of moral duty throughout the novel; he prioritizes survival and control above all else. In this instance, he is acting to secure the safety of his household members because their well-being directly impacts his own stability and future plans. He is calculating the best path to ensure they survive the night, viewing their rescue as a means to an end (the preservation of his family unit for his own benefit), rather than an end in itself based on inherent moral worth. Therefore, while the act looks like good-will on the surface, it is rooted in self-preservation and strategic thinking, consistent with his teleological worldview.
